summary: This RFC proposes using TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, to load an operating system or program onto a computer over the network at startup. Machines with no local disk can fetch what they need to boot.

eli5.summary: A computer with an empty brain asks another computer over the network for its instructions, using a simple way to hand over files.

questions: how to boot a computer over tftp
how does a diskless workstation boot over the network
subtitle: A proposal to use TFTP as the standard way for a machine to load its first code file from the network.

tldr.problem: Diskless machines bootstrapped over the network with a different, unstandardized loading method for each manufacturer, so one installation needed many boot servers.
tldr.mechanism: The booting machine sends a standard TFTP read request for its code file, optionally using RARP to learn its own internet address and ARP to find a server's hardware address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes this for the ARPA Internet community and asks for discussion. It also describes a ROM implementation of under 4K bytes.

today: The RFC presents itself as a proposed protocol for the ARPA Internet community, and the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown with no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It works together with RFC 903 (RARP).

sections.title: Why Boot Over the Network
sections.content:
Many systems, such as diskless workstations, load one or more code files across a network to start up. The protocol for these first files had not been standardized, and manufacturers used different methods. An installation supporting several kinds of systems needed a separate server for each boot mechanism, even though the machines could all talk freely once booted.

The RFC proposes TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) as the standard. It builds on IP, is easy to implement in the booting machine and in boot servers, and many operating systems already had TFTP servers. That TFTP is slow is not a serious concern, since it is needed only for the primary bootstrap and a secondary bootstrap could use a faster protocol. Only the network protocols are specified, not how a user starts a boot or which data-link network is used.
sections.eli5: Every computer maker had its own secret way to ask for starting instructions. This note says everyone should use one simple, shared way.

sections.title: Protocols Used by the Booter
sections.content:
The system being booted, called the booter, sends a standard TFTP read request (RRQ) naming the file to load. File names should avoid operating-system-specific conventions; alphanumeric characters should suffice. It then receives TFTP DATA packets and sends ACK and/or ERROR packets as TFTP specifies. TFTP runs over UDP over IP, so the booter must accept IP datagrams of up to 524 octets excluding the IP header (a TFTP DATA packet can be up to 516 octets and the UDP header is 8). The booter need not answer incoming read or write requests.

Two more protocols may be used. RARP lets the booter learn its internet address from its hardware address before sending the request, and ARP can find the server's hardware address if the server's internet address is known. Without a server address, a special broadcast internet address can be used, although no standard for internet broadcasting had been officially adopted.
sections.eli5: The booter asks for a file by name, and the server sends it in small pieces. The booter says 'got it' after each piece. If it does not know its own address, it asks the network first.

sections.title: An Example ROM Implementation
sections.content:
The author built this for a Motorola 68000 based workstation booting over Ethernet, with the code in ROM. The user types a file name and optionally the workstation's and a server's internet addresses. The code then (1) reads its Ethernet address from the interface, (2) broadcasts a RARP request if it has no internet address, failing the boot on timeout, (3) broadcasts an ARP request for the server's Ethernet address if a server address was given, otherwise using the Ethernet broadcast address, (4) if no server address was given, using a special local-subnet broadcast internet address, and (5) sending the TFTP RRQ.

Several servers may reply, so the booter does not give up on a TFTP ERROR packet. When the first valid DATA packet arrives, its source addresses are used for later ACK packets, and a later DATA from another server is answered with an ERROR.
sections.eli5: The example machine shouts for its address, shouts for a server, and then asks for the file. It listens to whichever server answers first and politely tells the others no.

sections.title: Size of the Code
sections.content:
A TFTP boot implementation can take up a lot of space if care is not taken, which matters when the code must fit in a limited ROM. The example implementation consists of less than 4K bytes of code, not counting the Ethernet device driver.

An editor's note on broadcasting strongly recommends that the all-ones local part of an internet address indicate broadcast in a network. For example, 1.255.255.255 in class A network 1, 128.1.255.255 in class B network 128.1, and 192.1.1.255 in class C network 192.1.1.
sections.eli5: The starter program lives in a tiny memory chip, so it has to be small. This one fits in less than 4K bytes.
